summary.title: Write Yourself a Scheme in 48 Hours
summary.one_liner: You learn to build a small Scheme interpreter in Haskell, covering parsing, evaluation, error handling, a REPL, mutable state, closures, file I/O and a standard library.
keywords: how to write a programming language interpreter
takeaways: Parse Scheme syntax into a data structure in Haskell
Evaluate Scheme expressions and add error checking and exceptions
Build a read-eval-print loop with basic I/O
Add variables, assignment, closures and environments, with mutable state in Haskell
Implement file I/O primitives and a small standard library using fold and unfold
summary.summary: This Wikibooks page is the table of contents and intro for a book-length tutorial, imported with permission from Jonathan Tang, that walks through writing a Scheme interpreter in Haskell. It is organised as chapters: setup, parsing, evaluation, error handling, a REPL, variables and mutable state, closures, file I/O, and a standard library built with fold and unfold, ending with further resources and exercise answers. The page notes the pace is brisk and it is a featured book, with a gentler Haskell Wikibook as a companion.
